source: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum — Eyewitness Testimony: Rwanda
extraction_note: The Norah Bagarinka transcript was supplied directly by the user and is stored verbatim. The USHMM page hosts several additional full-length transcripts that are copyrighted by USHMM; those are represented below as short paraphrased summaries (name, role, bio, and video link are factual/structural data, not reproduced prose) rather than reproduced at length.

testimonies.name: Norah Bagarinka
testimonies.bio: Norah Bagarinka, a Tutsi, was targeted during the 1994 Rwandan genocide. She survived, as many Tutsi did, by running and hiding for more than 100 days.
testimonies.transcript:
When we reached the roadblock, I found that the guy who was my gardener was the head in the roadblock and what they're telling that, “Tutsi here, Hutu here. If you know you are Tutsi, this side. If you know you are Hutu, this side.”

But then I started to ask myself, "What do I count myself? Do I go to my husband's side since I'm married to a Hutu? Maybe I had the right to stay on his side." But then immediately someone, one of the local people on the roadblock, came and pulled me, said, "Hey! You don't belong to that side if you're married to him — just here." So I was pulled to that side and they started up with a machete coming towards me. What I did, I raised up my hand and I said "Please, please don't kill me."

As I was putting my hands up, my gardener came, I can't remember whether this was a slasher or — it was something sharp because it cut my hand. And I fell down, and blood started shooting up, so my mother was trying to pull me up. They said — they hit her hard, she fell down, also, and the gardener came and said, "Okay, please," he pulled me up, said, "Leave her alone. I'm the one going to kill her because she was — I was digging for her and she was a very bad boss to me. She never paid me well. She never gave me food." In my mind, I thought I was going to be killed by him. He took us, like, my mother and other three ladies and took us aside on the other bush.

When we reached there, he got some leaves and bandaged my hand, and he told us, "Run! Run for your safety." And he apologized. He said, "Please, forgive me. This was the only way I could spare your lives."

testimonies.name: Jean-Philippe Ceppi
testimonies.bio: An independent journalist based in Kenya at the time of the genocide.
testimonies.summary: Ceppi described watching a Catholic sister in Kigali physically intervene to stop an armed group chasing down a young man, and recalled the scale of killing he witnessed — including a courtyard of hundreds of bodies — as what convinced him the word "genocide" applied.

testimonies.name: Gen. Roméo Dallaire
testimonies.bio: Canadian general who commanded the United Nations peacekeeping force deployed to Rwanda in late 1993.
testimonies.summary: Dallaire recalled finding a young boy alone amid decaying bodies during a patrol, and described the moment he recognized the same humanity in the child's eyes that he saw in his own son's.

testimonies.name: Alison Des Forges
testimonies.bio: A US-based human rights activist who had worked on Rwanda for years before the genocide and worked to publicize it as it unfolded.
testimonies.summary: Des Forges recounted a phone call with her Rwandan colleague Monique Mujawamariya as armed men closed in on her house; the call ended when her colleague asked her to look after her children before the line went dead.

testimonies.name: Mary "Fifi" Mukangoga
testimonies.bio: Sixteen years old when the genocide began; sought protection at a government office in Butare alongside other Tutsi, including her close friend Chantal.
testimonies.summary: Testimony given by her friend Chantal describes the sexual violence they endured while sheltering together, and Fifi's later death from HIV contracted through wartime rape.

testimonies.name: Damas Gisimba
testimonies.bio: Director of the Gisimba Memorial Center, an orphanage in Kigali, when the genocide began in April 1994.
testimonies.summary: Gisimba described hiding adults in the orphanage's ceiling during militia raids to protect them, and losing staff and people he was sheltering when the center was eventually attacked in June 1994.

testimonies.name: Stephen Rapp
testimonies.bio: Prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) from 2001 to 2006, and earlier a US Attorney.
testimonies.summary: Rapp described identifying closely with victims of the crimes he prosecuted, and his belief — shaped by tribunals from Yugoslavia to Rwanda to Sierra Leone — that perpetrators of mass atrocities must ultimately be held accountable.

testimonies.name: Clemantine Wamariya
testimonies.bio: Six years old when the genocide began in Rwanda.
testimonies.summary: Wamariya spoke about years spent as a refugee being treated as less than human, and about why survivors of atrocities have a responsibility to bear witness so that other injustices — including ongoing ones — are not ignored.

testimonies.name: Carl Wilkens
testimonies.bio: Directed the Adventist Development and Relief Agency International in Rwanda in 1994; stayed behind after his family evacuated to keep delivering aid.
testimonies.summary: Wilkens recounted a tense standoff in which a small group of gendarmes arrived at a compound under threat of massacre but said they couldn't stay, leaving him to decide whether to trust their officer enough to leave and seek reinforcements.
